identity.title: Extending Sequence Length is Not All You Need: Effective Integration of Multimodal Signals for Gene Expression Prediction

problem.claim: Improve gene expression prediction from DNA sequences by integrating multimodal epigenomic signals effectively.

gap.claim: Prior work emphasizes longer sequences for distal enhancers, while better integration of proximal multimodal signals has been overlooked; current models may lose performance on long sequences.

contributions.claim: Reports that long-sequence modeling can decrease performance for current gene-expression prediction models, and that proximal multimodal epigenomic signals are more essential.
Proposes Prism, which models combinations of high-dimensional epigenomic features as background chromatin states and applies backdoor adjustment to mitigate confounding.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that their work is the first to reveal performance degradation from long-sequence modeling in current models.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that proper multimodal epigenomic-signal modeling achieves state-of-the-art performance using only short sequences.
The authors report that carefully designed algorithms only mitigate, rather than eliminate, degradation caused by long sequences.
The authors report that signal types have distinct biological roles and that background chromatin patterns may introduce confounding effects.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames gene expression prediction from DNA sequences as challenging.
Notes that earlier work often extends sequences to capture distal enhancers.
Reports that long sequences can reduce performance and that proximal multimodal signals are more important but under-integrated.
Attributes risk to spurious associations with background chromatin patterns and introduces Prism with backdoor adjustment.
Reports state-of-the-art performance with short sequences when multimodal signals are properly modeled.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links distinct signal roles and background-pattern confounding to a specific integration design using state representations and backdoor adjustment.

lessons.interpretation: Separating biologically meaningful signals from nuisance structure can make the method rationale more explanatory than treating all modalities uniformly.
lessons.application: When proposing multimodal integration, explicitly characterize each modality’s role, identify possible nuisance patterns, and align the architecture or adjustment strategy with that distinction.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when signal roles or confounding pathways cannot be meaningfully specified from the available data.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, metrics, baselines, sequence lengths, or the magnitude and statistical conditions of the reported performance results.
It does not provide details sufficient to assess Prism’s implementation, backdoor assumptions, or the scope of the state-of-the-art comparison.
